RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Picts in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Highland Brochs & Hillforts, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Picts was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Highland Brochs & Hillforts, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Men in the hill country climb the stone stairs of the brochs in darkness, dragging ropes and flasks of watered wine. Their leather jerkins are stiff with cold, and supply sledges reach camp only after the fires have died. Spearmen trade what little silver they own for dry peat and a second blanket, knowing winter will last longer than the rations.

The chief's steward sends a sealed note from the glen: sheep counts are down, the wool tithe from eastern farms is incomplete, and the coastal trading party brought back less salt than promised. Offer the coastal merchants reduced tolls if they carry our hides south before the autumn gales. Keep the arrangement off the public ledger, because clan rivals watch every cart.
